summary: Brier Island's Western Light, on the westernmost point of Nova Scotia, was first lit in 1809; the wooden tower burned in 1944 and the present concrete tower was built that year.

lens.note: Fourth order dioptric lens, flashing white (18 s), fog signal, from 1992 (NSLPS)

structures.note: First tower, built by Isaiah Shaw; NSLPS and Lighthouse Friends both date its first light to 1809.
Rebuilt tower, white with three red bands by 1907-08. NSLPS gives 1832; Lighthouse Friends gives 1834 at a cost of 489 pounds. Burned in February 1944.
White octagonal concrete tower with horizontal red bands (Coast Guard list). Lighthouse Friends gives 18.3 m; NSLPS gives 60 ft; the Coast Guard list gives 16.7 m. See notes_for_editor.

access.note: Grounds open, tower closed (Lighthouse Friends). Reached by a gravel road across the island to a gate, then a short walk.

facts.agency: Municipality of the District of Digby (NSLPS). Lighthouse Friends says the Canadian Coast Guard owns it; see notes_for_editor.

events.note: Placed in operation, wooden tower built by Isaiah Shaw
Described as so vilely constructed and ill lighted that it was a hazard
House of Assembly committee reports the timber so decayed it may fall within a year
Tower rebuilt (NSLPS: by 1832; Lighthouse Friends: replacement built 1834 at a cost of 489 pounds)
Steam fog whistle established on the south side of the tower on 1 March 1873
Separate light on the north point of the island (Grand Passage) put in operation, January 1901; not this station
On 1 November 1902 changed from a fixed white light to a group-revolving catoptric white light
Keepers' dwellings built at the two light stations on the island, by contract at $3,150
New fog-alarm building with a three-inch diaphone (Lighthouse Friends)
Tower given three red horizontal bands; Department's report for 1907-08 lists Brier Island among lighthouses repainted white and red
Diaphone placed above the building on a level with the whistle; room extended to encase it (Department's report for 1908-09)
SS Bona Vista driven ashore on Brier Island in a heavy gale, 16 March 1912
Third order dioptric lens, group flashing white 15 s, air diaphone, 1922 to 1941
Wooden tower destroyed by fire in February 1944; origin not known (Lighthouse Friends, quoting a newspaper of the next day)
Current concrete octagonal tower built after the fire
Fourth order dioptric lens, flashing white 18 s, fog signal
Designated a heritage lighthouse under the Heritage Lighthouse Protection Act, December 2021

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1944 date is the present concrete tower. The first light is dated 1809 by Lighthouse Friends and NSLPS, and the record's Rowlett and Wikidata entries agree on 1809 for the first light.
The record's 29.0 m (map source) conflicts with the Coast Guard list's 22.2 m. The Coast Guard list is used.
Lighthouse Friends gives 18.3 m; NSLPS gives 60 ft (about 18.3 m); the Coast Guard list gives 16.7 m for the structure above ground. The story states all three.
Checked on the 1907 page image (printed p. 174, scan 183): Peters, John N sits on the row for Brier Island Light, appointed June 6, 1901, salary 400.
Lighthouse Friends' body text dates Wickerson Lent's interview to 2001; its reference list gives Passages, August-September 2002. The story gives the text date and notes the reference-list date.

notes_for_editor: No USLHS roster exists for Canada. Brier Island has two lights: the Western Light at the west point (this station) and the Grand Passage light on the north point, which the Department's reports treat as a separate station with its own keeper; the 1905 dwellings and some keeper entries cover both, so check which light a keeper served. (1) Heights: Lighthouse Friends gives the concrete tower as 18.3 m; NSLPS gives 60 ft (about 18.3 m); the Coast Guard list gives a tower height of 16.7 m by column position; the record gives 18.0 m. The story uses Lighthouse Friends with NSLPS. (2) The 1832 replacement: NSLPS gives 1832; Lighthouse Friends gives 1834 at 489 pounds; both are cited. (3) Keepers: Lighthouse Friends' keeper list and its text disagree about the Suthern family (Joseph Suthern 1867-1883 on the list; a son, Frank Suthern, credited with the fog whistle from 1874 in the text; John F. Suthern 1874-1901 on the fog-alarm list). The sources read do not settle who was who. The NSLPS list adds 'Suthern, John' with a date that reads 1855 in the OCR. (4) Department keeper tables are OCR'd in blocks; 'Peters, John N [Brier Lsland Light' (scan 183) and 'Brier Island, Fog Whistle June 6, 1901' (scan 174, printed page uncertain) are matched by line position, and the 1901 date is read by column position and may belong to another name. (5) Ownership: NSLPS says the Municipality of the District of Digby; Lighthouse Friends says the Canadian Coast Guard owns the light and its visitor note may be out of date. (6) The 1944 fire is known from Lighthouse Friends quoting a newspaper of the next day; the newspaper was not seen and no date beyond February 1944 is given. The keeper's name 'Albert Walsh (Welch)' is printed as Lighthouse Friends gives it. (7) The Islands History page for Brier Island returned only a stub and was not used. (8) The Parks Canada heritage record (16412) was not read; the 2021 designation comes from Lighthouse Friends. (9) Chronicling America returned no Brier Island pages for 1944, and no Nova Scotia newspaper archive was reachable. (10) The Bona Vista wreck is in the 1912 casualty list (scan 237), read as 'driven ashore on Brier island'; it is the only March 1912 Nova Scotia loss found in that list, and the Parks Canada statement for Boar's Head dates two other losses to 16 March 1911 and 1912 without names. Fact-check 2026-10-27 (independent checker): the 1905 keepers' table row for Morrell (Brier Island, Fog Whistle, June 6, 1901) is on printed p. 161 (scan 174), not p. 21 as the earlier note had it; footnote 8 corrected. The 1907 keepers' table row for Peters is confirmed on the page image. The 1908-09 diaphone entry (printed p. 55, scan 62) concerns Brier Island and reads 'above the building, on a level with the whistle'; the story now says so. The 1902 report (printed 1903) records the 1 November 1902 change, so the footnote's fiscal year 1901-02 is the report's own label. The Bona Vista page (printed p. 230, scan 237) was not image-checked; the wreck is placed on the island, not at the light.
